answer.answerText:
Yes. For multiple occupancies, apply the applicable Table 403.1 fixture ratio(s) to each occupancy’s occupant load (ordinarily dividing each total occupant load equally by sex), sum the resulting fractional requirements for each fixture type across the occupancies, and then round that sum up to the next whole number. The 50/50 sex split need not be used only where approved statistical data supports another distribution. The Building Code—not Table 403.1—determines the occupancy classifications and occupant loads.

The multipurpose room may use Assembly fixture requirements if it is in fact used for assembly, has an occupant load under 75, and is accessory to another occupancy. BC 303.1.3 classifies such a room as Group B or as part of the principal occupancy, but expressly permits its plumbing fixtures to be calculated under the Assembly requirements. The separately supplied PC 403.1 permission is limited to a building or nonaccessory tenant space under its stated Section 303.1, Exception 2 condition; it is not independent authority for this potentially accessory room. The Assembly fixture category and the Table 403.1 ratios are not included in the supplied evidence, so no final fixture count can be calculated.

Material unresolved items are the actual functions and Building Code classifications of the B, F, and S rooms; occupant load for each occupancy; confirmation that the multipurpose room is accessory; the applicable Assembly category; whether facilities are proposed to serve more than one space; and the number and availability of existing fixtures. The selected evidence does not establish permission for shared facilities to serve the identified occupancies.
answer.conclusion: Yes. For multiple occupancies, apply the applicable Table 403.1 fixture ratio(s) to each occupancy’s occupant load (ordinarily dividing each total occupant load equally by sex), sum the resulting fractional requirements for each fixture type across the occupancies, and then round that sum up to the next whole number. The 50/50 sex split need not be used only where approved statistical data supports another distribution. The Building Code—not Table 403.1—determines the occupancy classifications and occupant loads.

supportedPoints.heading: Add fractions before rounding for multiple occupancies
supportedPoints.explanation: For each fixture type, apply the applicable Table 403.1 ratio or ratios to the occupant load of each sex for each occupancy. For multiple occupancies, sum the resulting fractional requirements for each occupancy first, then round the sum up to the next whole number. Ordinarily, divide the total occupant load equally by sex; a different distribution is allowed only where approved statistical data supports it. Group B office calculations use the total occupant load on a given floor.

supportedPoints.heading: Fixture table follows Building Code occupancy and load determinations
supportedPoints.explanation: Plumbing fixtures are required by occupancy type and Table 403.1 minimums. The New York City Building Code determines both occupancy classification and occupant load; an occupancy type not shown in Table 403.1 is considered individually by the commissioner.

supportedPoints.heading: Accessory assembly room may use Assembly fixture calculation
supportedPoints.explanation: A room or space used for assembly with fewer than 75 occupants and accessory to another occupancy is classified as Group B or as part of that occupancy, but its plumbing-fixture count is permitted to be calculated under the Assembly-occupancy requirements. This conclusion is conditional on the room actually being an accessory assembly space.

supportedPoints.heading: Separate PC Assembly permission has a limited scope
supportedPoints.explanation: The supplied PC 403.1 text separately permits an Assembly fixture calculation for a building or nonaccessory tenant space used for assembly by fewer than 75 persons and classified as Group B under the stated Building Code provision. Its stated scope does not independently govern the potentially accessory room described here.

1004.3 1004.3 Fixed seating. For areas having fixed seats and aisles, the occupant load shall be determined by the number of fixed seats installed therein. The occupant load for areas in which fixed seating is not installed, such as waiting spaces, shall be determined in accordance with Section 1004.1.3 and added to the number of fixed seats. The occupant load of wheelchair spaces and the associated companion seat shall be based on one occupant for each wheelchair space and one occupant for the associated companion seat provided in accordance with Section 1108.2.3. For areas having fixed seating without dividing arms, the occupant load shall be not less than the number of seats based on one person for each 18 inches (457.2 mm) of seating length. The occupant load of seating booths shall be based on one person for each 24 inches (609.6 mm) of booth seat length measured at the backrest of the seating booth.

1004.1 1004.1 Design occupant load. Design occupant load. The minimum dimension of such corridors shall be sufficient to accommodate the total occupant load discharging into such corridors, but shall in no case be less than 5 feet (1524 mm) in minimum dimension; and 5. In addition to Conditions 1 through 4 above, one of the following conditions shall be met: 5.1. Each of the interior exit stairways and ramps serving such story shall be protected by a smokeproof enclosure in accordance with Section 909.20; 5.2. The corridor or portions of the corridor serving the rooms, areas or spaces that are accessory to the Group R-2 occupancy shall be pressurized in accordance with requirements that are applicable to interior exit stairways. Connecting interior exit stairways need not be pressurized unless otherwise required by this code; 5.3. All passenger elevators serving the rooms, areas, or spaces that are accessory to the Group R-2 occupancy shall comply with occupant self-evacuation elevator requirements in Section 3008.1 through 3008.11; or 5.4. One additional exit stairway meeting the requirements of Sections 1009 and 1023 shall be provided in addition to the minimum number of exits required by Section 1006 . The total width of any combination of remaining exit stairways with one exit stairway removed shall not be less than the total width required by Section 1005.3. Rooms, areas or spaces that do not comply with the conditions in Sections 1004.1.1.2.1 and 1004.1.1.2.2, or Section 1004.1.1.2.3 where applicable, shall have occupant loads calculated cumulatively per story and be classified as Occupancy Group A.

DWELLING UNIT. A single unit consisting of one or more habitable rooms and occupied or arranged to be occupied as a unit separate from all other units within a dwelling. EXIT ACCESS. That portion of a means of egress system that leads from any occupied portion of a building or structure to an exit. FOOD COURT. See Section 402.2. INTERIOR EXIT STAIRWAY. An exit component that serves to meet one or more means of egress design requirements, such as required number of exits or exit access travel distance, and provides for a protected path of egress travel to the exit discharge or public way. NURSING HOMES . See Section 308 . 2 . 2 . OCCUPANT LOAD . The number of persons for which the means of egress of a building or portion thereof is designed . PARKING GARAGE. A structure or portion of a structure, other than a private garage or carport, used for the parking or storage of motor vehicles. WHEELCHAIR SPACE . A space for a single wheelchair and its occupant .

403.2 403.2 Separate facilities. Where plumbing fixtures are required, separate facilities shall be provided for each sex. Exceptions: 1. Separate facilities shall not be required for dwelling units and sleeping units. 2. In structures or tenant spaces where combined employee and public toilet facilities are provided in accordance with Section 403.3, separate facilities shall not be required where the total number of employees, customers, patrons and visitors is 30 or fewer. 3. In structures or tenant spaces where required toilet facilities for only employee use are provided in accordance with Section 403.3, separate facilities shall not be required where the total number of employees is 30 or fewer. 4. testCase.title: Movable seating and a proposed lower stated occupant load

projectContext.existingDocumentation: Group B floor documented at 1 occupant per 100 square feet
projectContext.reportedCalculatedLoad: More than 200 occupants overall, with no individual room at 75 or more
projectContext.proposedReduction: Count selected seats and treat some functions as nonsimultaneous

exactPassages: Where an area under consideration contains multiple functions having different occupant load factors, the design occupant load for such area shall be based on the floor area of each function calculated independently.

For areas without fixed seating, the occupant load shall be not less than that number determined by dividing the floor area under consideration by the occupant load factor assigned to the function of the space as set forth in Table 1004.1.3.

Where the actual number of occupants of any space will be significantly lower than listed in Table 1004.1.3 , the commissioner may establish a lower basis for the determination of the number of occupants.

For areas having fixed seats and aisles, the occupant load shall be determined by the number of fixed seats installed therein. The occupant load for areas in which fixed seating is not installed, such as waiting spaces, shall be determined in accordance with Section 1004.1.3 and added to the number of fixed seats.

testCase.question: For this 2022-code evaluation scenario, may the conference floor's occupant load be documented by counting selected movable seats, omitting lounge and break functions as nonsimultaneous, and retaining the existing 1:100 load without a commissioner-established lower basis?
testCase.expectedConclusion: No. BC 1004.3 uses the number of installed seats for fixed seating, while areas without fixed seating must be determined under BC 1004.1.3. BC 1004.1.2 requires the floor area of each function with a different occupant-load factor to be calculated independently. A lower actual-occupancy basis is not automatic: BC 1004.1.3.1 states that the commissioner may establish it when actual occupancy will be significantly lower. The selected evidence does not establish that the lounge and break areas may be omitted as nonsimultaneous, nor does it resolve filing type, place-of-assembly status, posted occupancy, or egress capacity. Those conclusions require the actual plans, functions, use assumptions, existing records, and applicable official authority.

expectedUncertainty.description: The selected passages reject automatic movable-seat counting and require independent functional calculations, but a final occupant load and any approved lower basis depend on missing plans, facts, and commissioner action.

answer.answerText:
No, the proposed reduction cannot be established from the supplied evidence. Because the seats are movable rather than fixed, counting selected seats is not the fixed-seating method. Areas without fixed seating must be assigned an occupant load no lower than the applicable Table 1004.1.3 function-based floor-area calculation. If the conference, soft-seating, and coffee-break/lounge areas have different applicable factors, each function’s area must be calculated independently.

The supplied provisions do not establish whether lounge and break functions may be excluded based on claimed nonsimultaneous use. Whether and how those functions are available for simultaneous use remains material to the proposed documentation approach. The existing 1:100 basis can be retained only if it is no lower than the required calculation for every applicable function; the supplied evidence lacks both the table factors and the function-by-function area allocation needed to test that result.

A lower-than-table result may be used only if the commissioner establishes a lower basis where the actual number of occupants will be significantly lower than the table result. No such commissioner-established basis is provided. For means of egress, the design occupant load is the largest number computed under the applicable calculation provisions, unless one of the referenced permissions applies.

The reported overall load above 200 does not itself resolve the calculation, and the stated absence of any individual room at 75 or more does not require analysis under the supplied Certificate of Operation provision. That provision concerns indoor assembly occupancies used or intended for use by 75 persons or more; the project facts state no individual room reaches that threshold.
answer.conclusion: No, the proposed reduction cannot be established from the supplied evidence. Because the seats are movable rather than fixed, counting selected seats is not the fixed-seating method. Areas without fixed seating must be assigned an occupant load no lower than the applicable Table 1004.1.3 function-based floor-area calculation. If the conference, soft-seating, and coffee-break/lounge areas have different applicable factors, each function’s area must be calculated independently.

supportedPoints.heading: Different functions require independent area calculations
supportedPoints.explanation: Where an area contains multiple functions with different occupant-load factors, the design occupant load must be based on the floor area of each function calculated independently. Thus, the conference, soft-seating, and coffee-break/lounge functions cannot be treated as one undifferentiated area if their applicable factors differ.

supportedPoints.heading: Movable seats do not use the fixed-seat method
supportedPoints.explanation: The fixed-seat method applies to areas having fixed seats and aisles. Where fixed seating is not installed, the occupant load is determined under the areas-without-fixed-seating rule and added to any fixed-seat count. On the stated fact that seating is movable, a selected movable-seat count does not establish occupant load under the fixed-seating provision.

supportedPoints.heading: Unfixed areas have a table-based minimum
supportedPoints.explanation: For an area without fixed seating, occupant load must be not less than the floor area divided by the Table 1004.1.3 factor assigned to the space’s function. The supplied evidence does not include the applicable table entries or function-specific area allocation, so it cannot establish whether the existing 1:100 basis meets each applicable minimum.

supportedPoints.heading: A lower basis requires commissioner action
supportedPoints.explanation: Where actual occupancy will be significantly lower than the Table 1004.1.3 result, the commissioner may establish a lower basis. Because no commissioner-established lower basis is provided, this provision does not support the proposed reduction below the otherwise applicable table-based calculation.

supportedPoints.heading: Egress uses the largest applicable computed load
supportedPoints.explanation: For means-of-egress requirements, the design occupant load is the largest number computed under Section 1004.1.3, unless otherwise permitted by the listed provisions, including the commissioner modification provision.

sources.text: Where an area under consideration contains multiple functions having different occupant load factors, the design occupant load for such area shall be based on the floor area of each function calculated independently.

For areas without fixed seating, the occupant load shall be not less than that number determined by dividing the floor area under consideration by the occupant load factor assigned to the function of the space as set forth in Table 1004.1.3.

Where the actual number of occupants of any space will be significantly lower than listed in Table 1004.1.3 , the commissioner may establish a lower basis for the determination of the number of occupants.

For areas having fixed seats and aisles, the occupant load shall be determined by the number of fixed seats installed therein. The occupant load for areas in which fixed seating is not installed, such as waiting spaces, shall be determined in accordance with Section 1004.1.3 and added to the number of fixed seats.

1004.1 1004.1 Design occupant load. Design occupant load. In determining means of egress requirements, the number of occupants for whom means of egress facilities shall be provided shall be established by the largest number computed in accordance with Section 1004.1.3, unless otherwise permitted by Section 1004.1.3.1, 1004.1.3.2 or 1004.2.

1004.1.3.2 1004.1.3.2 Unlisted functions. Where data regarding the square feet area per person for a function is not listed in Table 1004.1.3 , the occupant load shall be established by a registered design professional, subject to the approval of the commissioner.

1004.1.1.2.3 1004.1.1.2.3 Group R-2 accessory spaces as primary function on a story. Where the aggregate Group R-2 occupancy accessory area of all rooms, areas or spaces, including outdoor spaces that are not provided with independent means of egress and that do not converge into interior means of egress, exceed 50 percent of the building area of the story in which they are located, and the total number of occupants on such story exceeds 150 persons, the following conditions shall apply: 1. The interior corridors or portions thereof serving such accessory spaces shall be constructed as public corridors in accordance with Table 1020.1.2 with 1-hour fire-resistance-rated fire barriers, and 2-hour fire-resistance-rated fire barriers where a dead-end corridor exceeds 40 feet (12 192 mm) in length; 2. Access to the corridors shall be limited to those necessary for exit access through the corridor from normally occupied spaces. Direct openings from the mechanical, electrical and other storage spaces shall not be permitted, except that access to the corridor may be provided through a vestibule constructed with fire barriers, with a minimum fire-resistance rating consistent with the required hourly rating for the corridor; 3. Corridors or portions thereof serving such accessory spaces shall be sufficient to accommodate a total occupant load on the basis of 3 square feet (0.28 m 2 ) per person; 4. The minimum dimension of such corridors shall be sufficient to accommodate the total occupant load discharging into such corridors, but shall in no case be less than 5 feet (1524 mm) in minimum dimension; and 5. In addition to Conditions 1 through 4 above, one of the following conditions shall be met: 5.1. Each of the interior exit stairways and ramps serving such story shall be protected by a smokeproof enclosure in accordance with Section 909.20; 5.2. The corridor or portions of the corridor serving the rooms, areas or spaces that are accessory to the Group R-2 occupancy shall be pressurized in accordance with requirements that are applicable to interior exit stairways. Connecting interior exit stairways need not be pressurized unless otherwise required by this code; 5.3. All passenger elevators serving the rooms, areas, or spaces that are accessory to the Group R-2 occupancy shall comply with occupant self-evacuation elevator requirements in Section 3008.1 through 3008.11; or 5.4. One additional exit stairway meeting the requirements of Sections 1009 and 1023 shall be provided in addition to the minimum number of exits required by Section 1006 . The total width of any combination of remaining exit stairways with one exit stairway removed shall not be less than the total width required by Section 1005.3. Rooms, areas or spaces that do not comply with the conditions in Sections 1004.1.1.2.1 and 1004.1.1.2.2, or Section 1004.1.1.2.3 where applicable, shall have occupant loads calculated cumulatively per story and be classified as Occupancy Group A.

1004.1.1.2 1004.1.1.2 Cumulative occupant loads in Group R-2 occupancies. Rooms, areas or spaces that are accessory to a Group R-2 occupancy and that comply with the conditions below may have occupant loads calculated individually per room, area, or space, and be classified as Occupancy Group R-2.

CERTIFICATE OF OPERATION. A certificate issued by the department upon satisfactory inspection of a specific piece of hoisting equipment to ensure that the equipment is in compliance with this code. DWELLING UNIT. A single unit consisting of one or more habitable rooms and occupied or arranged to be occupied as a unit separate from all other units within a dwelling. EXIT ACCESS. That portion of a means of egress system that leads from any occupied portion of a building or structure to an exit. FIXED SEATING. Furniture or fixture designed and installed for the use of sitting and secured in place including bench-type seats and seats with or without backs or arm rests. INTERIOR EXIT STAIRWAY. An exit component that serves to meet one or more means of egress design requirements, such as required number of exits or exit access travel distance, and provides for a protected path of egress travel to the exit discharge or public way. OCCUPANT LOAD . The number of persons for which the means of egress of a building or portion thereof is designed . PARKING GARAGE. A structure or portion of a structure, other than a private garage or carport, used for the parking or storage of motor vehicles. WHEELCHAIR SPACE . A space for a single wheelchair and its occupant .
402.8.2 402.8.2 Occupant load. The calculated occupant load used to determine the required number of means of egress shall be in accordance with this section.

303.7 303.7 Certificate of Operation. A Certificate of Operation shall be required, as per Section 28-117.1 , for the following assembly occupancies: 1. Indoor assembly occupancies used or intended for use by 75 persons or more, including open spaces at 20 feet (6096 mm) or more above or below grade plane, such as roofs or roof terraces. 2. Outdoor assembly occupancies used and intended for use by 200 persons or more. Section BC 304: Business Group B

1108.2.3 1108.2.3 Companion seats. At least one companion seat complying with ICC A117.1, including Section 802.7 (Companion Seat), shall be provided for each wheelchair space required by Sections 1108.2.2.1 through 1108.2.2.3 of this code.

testCase.question: An existing prior-code Group B building has a previously approved legacy fire-alarm system. A proposed enlargement does not change the stated use or occupancy, but the resulting Group B gross area may exceed 100,000 square feet. The height of the highest occupied floor above the lowest level of Fire Department vehicle access has not been confirmed. Does the selected 2022 Building Code evidence automatically require replacement of the entire legacy system, and what additional facts determine the required scope?
testCase.expectedConclusion: The enlargement does not, by itself, prove that the entire legacy system must be replaced. BC 901.9.1 requires additions and alterations to existing systems to comply with new-system requirements without automatically requiring the entire existing system to comply, subject to the additional triggers in Sections 901.9.2 through 901.9.6. BC 901.9.3 requires fire-protection systems in enlarged portions and where Chapter 9 would require them for new construction. If the resulting Group B occupancy exceeds 100,000 square feet and the highest occupied floor is 75 feet or less above the lowest Fire Department vehicle-access level, BC 907.2.2.2 requires the identified smoke-detection, fire-alarm, and emergency voice/alarm systems for the qualifying Group B occupancy; that requirement cannot automatically be limited to only the enlarged portion. On the stated facts, BC 901.9.2 is not triggered unless the asserted absence of an occupancy or use change is incorrect. A main-use or dominant-occupancy change applies to the entire building; a space occupancy-classification or usage change applies throughout that space. The selected evidence does not determine whether the legacy equipment can be extended, interfaced, or retained, or whether technical conditions ultimately require modification or replacement.

expectedUncertainty.description: The selected passages establish upgrade triggers and scope principles, but they cannot establish whether the existing system may be retained or must be replaced without project-specific system, occupancy, area, height, and compatibility facts.

answer.answerText:
No. On the stated facts, the selected evidence does not automatically require replacement of the entire previously approved legacy fire-alarm system merely because the building is enlarged or may exceed 100,000 square feet. For work on an existing system, the addition, alteration, renovation, or repair must meet new-system requirements, but the existing system need not be brought wholly into compliance unless one of the specified additional provisions applies; the work also cannot make the installation unsafe, hazardous, or overloaded.

The enlargement itself must receive any fire-protection systems that Chapter 9 would require in new construction for the enlarged space or building. If the resulting Group B occupancy exceeds 100,000 gross square feet **and** the highest occupied floor is 75 feet or less above the lowest Fire Department vehicle-access level, BC 907.2.2.2 requires automatic smoke detection connected to the fire-alarm system and an emergency voice/alarm communication system that initiates a total-evacuation signal. That is a building/occupancy trigger stated separately from the rule for the enlarged portion; the selected evidence does not say the resulting required systems may be limited to the enlargement. It also does not, by itself, prescribe wholesale replacement rather than a compliant extension, modification, or integration of the legacy system.

A whole-building new-system obligation is expressly stated where there is a change in the building's main use or dominant occupancy. A change in occupancy-group classification or usage instead triggers systems throughout the affected space. The stated no-change premise therefore does not activate either of those particular change-based paths, subject to confirming that no such change occurs.

Material facts needed to establish scope are the actual highest-occupied-floor height relative to Fire Department vehicle access; final total Group B gross area; exact enlargement and fire-alarm work scope; whether the existing system has sufficient capacity and compatibility to add the required detection/voice functions without becoming overloaded or unsafe; and whether any occupancy classification or space-usage change occurs. Other Chapter 9 triggers may also independently affect the required system scope, but the supplied evidence does not identify them. Separately, the supplied Administrative Code text says that if the enlargement increases a prior-code building's floor surface area by more than 110 percent over existing floor surface area, the entire building must comply as if newly erected; that percentage must be calculated using the supplied definition and exclusions before relying on the prior-code status.

This is an interpretation of the selected evidence, not an approval determination.
answer.conclusion: No. On the stated facts, the selected evidence does not automatically require replacement of the entire previously approved legacy fire-alarm system merely because the building is enlarged or may exceed 100,000 square feet. For work on an existing system, the addition, alteration, renovation, or repair must meet new-system requirements, but the existing system need not be brought wholly into compliance unless one of the specified additional provisions applies; the work also cannot make the installation unsafe, hazardous, or overloaded.

supportedPoints.heading: Existing-system work is not automatically a whole-system upgrade
supportedPoints.explanation: Additions, alterations, renovations, and repairs to an existing fire-protection system must conform to requirements for new systems, but the existing system need not comply with all current-code requirements unless Sections 901.9.2 through 901.9.6 otherwise require it. The work may not make the existing installation unsafe, hazardous, or overloaded.

supportedPoints.heading: Change-based whole-building and space triggers
supportedPoints.explanation: Chapter 9 fire-protection systems must be provided throughout the entire building as if newly erected when the main use or dominant occupancy changes. They must be provided throughout a space when that space's occupancy-group classification or usage changes. On the stated no-change premise, these specific triggers are not established.

supportedPoints.heading: Enlargement requires new-construction systems where applicable
supportedPoints.explanation: Fire-protection systems must be provided in enlarged portions and wherever Chapter 9 would require those systems in new construction for a space or building. This establishes the enlarged-portion rule and a separate building-or-space new-construction trigger.

supportedPoints.heading: Large-area Group B fire-alarm trigger
supportedPoints.explanation: For a Group B occupancy exceeding 100,000 gross square feet in a building whose highest occupied floor is 75 feet or less above the lowest Fire Department vehicle-access level, automatic smoke detection connected to an automatic fire-alarm system and a total-evacuation emergency voice/alarm communication system are required. The supplied provision does not limit these required systems to the enlarged portion or prescribe complete replacement of an existing system.

supportedPoints.heading: Prior-code building enlargement exceeding 110 percent
supportedPoints.explanation: If the completed work increases a prior-code building's floor surface area by more than 110 percent over existing floor surface area, the entire building must comply as if it were newly erected. The calculation uses gross area of all horizontal floor and roof surfaces, including the listed levels, subject to the stated exclusions for certain removed floors and recently installed floors.

supportingPassages.selectedText: 28-101.4.5 § 28-101.4.5 Work that increases existing floor surface area of a prior code building by more than 110 percent. Notwithstanding sections 28-101.4.3 and 28-102.4.3 or any other provision of this code that would authorize alterations of prior code buildings in accordance with the 1968 building code or prior codes, where the proposed work at the completion of construction will increase the amount of floor surface area of a prior code building by more than 110%, over the amount of existing floor surface area, such entire building shall be made to comply with the provisions of this code as if it were a new building hereafter erected. See section 28-105.2 for permits for such work. Exceptions. When determining the amount of existing floor surface area for the purposes of section 28-101.4.5 , the following shall be excluded from the measured square footage of floor surface area: 1. The square footage of floors removed during the course of the work when such floors are removed together with the supporting beams, joists, decking and slabs on grade. 2. The square footage of any floor that was installed together with the supporting beams, joists, decking and slabs on grade less than 12 months prior to submission of the application for construction document approval for the proposed work. For the purposes of this exception, floors installed pursuant to a work permit signed off less than 12 months before such submission shall not be counted as existing floor surface area.

BC 1101.3 addresses accessibility in alterations and changes of use or occupancy in prior-code buildings; it is not the authority for a Certificate of Occupancy amendment exception. If the project is an alteration in a prior-code building and is considered a change in the space's Building Code occupancy classification or zoning use group, BC 1101.3.1 conditionally requires the Chapter 11 accessible features and construction throughout the space, including its immediate entrances.
